text: An idempotency key is a unique identifier used to prevent duplicate operations. The client sends the key with a request so that retries do not repeat an operation that already succeeded.
A dead letter queue stores messages that could not be processed successfully. Messages land there after exceeding the maximum number of delivery attempts, so operators can inspect and replay them.

A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing dependency once errors cross a threshold. While the breaker is open, requests fail fast instead of waiting on timeouts, and a half-open state probes for recovery.
Exponential backoff increases the wait time between retries after each failed attempt. Adding random jitter to the delay spreads retries out and avoids synchronized retry storms.
Consistent hashing maps keys and nodes onto the same hash ring. When a node joins or leaves, only the keys adjacent to it move, instead of nearly every key being reassigned.

The CAP theorem states that during a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability. Partition tolerance is not optional for systems that communicate over a network.
A write-ahead log records every change before it is applied to the data files. After a crash the database replays the log to restore a consistent state.
Eventual consistency guarantees that replicas converge to the same value once updates stop. Reads may return stale data for a short time after a write.
Raft elects a leader through randomized election timeouts. A candidate becomes leader after receiving votes from a majority of the cluster, and the leader then replicates log entries to followers.
The token bucket algorithm limits request rate by adding tokens at a fixed rate up to a maximum capacity. Each request consumes a token, which permits short bursts while enforcing an average rate.
Sharding splits a dataset horizontally across multiple databases by a shard key. Each shard holds a subset of rows, which spreads storage and write load across machines.
A Bloom filter is a probabilistic data structure that tests set membership. It can return false positives but never false negatives, and it uses far less memory than storing the elements.

The transactional outbox pattern writes outgoing events to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change. A separate relay publishes rows from the outbox to the message broker.
Backpressure lets a slow consumer signal producers to reduce their sending rate. Without it, buffers between stages grow until memory is exhausted.

Two-phase commit coordinates an atomic transaction across participants. In the prepare phase every participant votes, and in the commit phase the coordinator tells all participants to commit or abort.

Vector clocks track causality between events in a distributed system. Each node keeps a counter per node, and comparing two vectors shows whether one event happened before another or they are concurrent.
A message queue decouples producers from consumers by buffering messages until a consumer processes them. Queues often support acknowledgements and redelivery.
Retries help clients recover from transient network failures. Retrying a non-idempotent request can apply the same operation twice, which is why payment APIs need careful retry handling.
HTTP caching uses headers such as Cache-Control and ETag to let clients reuse responses. A conditional request with If-None-Match returns 304 Not Modified when the resource is unchanged.
Blue-green deployment runs two identical production environments. Traffic switches from the old environment to the new one at once, and rolling back means switching traffic back.
